title: AI in Mammography Screening: A Scoping Review of Integration Models and Reporting Practices
abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly deployed in mammography screening, but they occupy structurally different roles in the reading pathway. An AI system may substitute for a second human reader, partition the screening cohort so that low-risk examinations receive reduced or no human reading, prompt a reader concurrently as a reading aid, operate after human reading as a safety net, or, as a benchmark condition, operate standalone with no human reader in the loop. Each role carries different failure modes, workload implications, and governance requirements. However, the terminology used to describe these roles—including triage, decision referral, pre-screening, rule-out, and autonomous—is applied inconsistently to overlapping configurations across the literature. Existing syntheses have primarily compared these positions on pooled detection, recall, and workload outcomes, requiring heterogeneous configurations to be collapsed into a small number of poolable categories. Such approaches cannot characterize how AI roles are defined, configured, and operationalized. This scoping review will map AI integration roles in screening mammography, including their terminology, configuration and thresholding strategies, reported outcomes for each, and gaps in the evidence and in reporting. The review will follow JBI scoping review methodology and will be reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore will be searched from 1 January 2016 to the date of the final search, supplemented by trial registries (including ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO ICTRP), preprint servers, and forward and backward citation chasing of included studies. Eligible studies will evaluate one or more defined AI configurations applied to a screening mammography case set in which the AI system’s position in the reading pathway is specified, regardless of study design. Consistent with scoping review methodology, no formal critical appraisal will be conducted and studies will not be excluded on quality grounds. Case-set assembly will instead be charted as a prespecified variable, and performance results from consecutive screening cohorts will not be combined with those from enriched or two-gate case sets. Expected outputs include a role-by-terminology matrix characterizing definitional variation, a role-by-outcome matrix identifying unreported outcomes, a summary of threshold and operating-point selection by role, and an evidence-gap map highlighting under-represented populations and screening-program structures. No meta-analysis will be conducted. Search strategies, screening decisions, and the completed charting table will be deposited publicly on the associated OSF project.

title: Generalist Open-World Temporal Perception
abstract: The next generation of artificial intelligence systems will likely be natively temporal and multimodal in both inputs and outputs: able to converse, perceive, predict, reason, and synthesize through a shared world representation. Realizing this requires a temporal perceptual substrate integrating sensory streams, language, and structured outputs within a multimodal world model. We seek a generalist open-world perceptual system that represents biological forms, natural physical structures, and artifacts, and their interactions, as a coherent, temporally persistent process. The model should infer geometry, articulation, semantics, interaction structure, and uncertainty from raw multimodal streams; maintain identity through occlusion and viewpoint change; generalize across species, forms, mechanisms, and materials; and abstain or expand its ontology when encountering the unknown. The objective is a structured world state supporting understanding, prediction, counterfactual reasoning, and controllable synthesis. Recent work suggests that some cross-modal and reasoning-like capabilities can emerge from large-scale generative video pretraining, reminiscent of language-model scaling. Yet these capabilities are often accessed through language probes or expressed through photorealistic video, leaving explicit semantic, geometric, or temporal structure largely unexposed. This paper articulates an alternative and complementary paradigm: perception and synthesis as distinct conditionings within a shared Generalist Open-World Temporal Perception Architecture (GOWTPA). Recognition, structured prediction, and simulation arise as different conditionings of the same generative substrate, while reasoning and embodiment-specific policies build upon the resulting world state. This positions generalist temporal perception as a potential foundation layer for broader multimodal intelligence and physical AI.

This paper articulates an alternative and complementary paradigm: perception and synthesis as distinct conditionings within a shared Generalist Open-World Temporal Perception Architecture (GOWTPA). Recognition, structured prediction, and simulation arise as different conditionings of the same generative substrate, while reasoning and embodiment-specific policies build upon the resulting world state. This positions generalist temporal perception as a potential foundation layer for broader multimodal intelligence and physical AI.

title: ProcArena: A Multi-Scenario Benchmark for LLMs on Direct and Interactive PL/SQL Development from Natural Language
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong potential for translating natural-language (NL) requirements into PL/SQL programs, attracting increasing attention from the database community. However, existing NL-to-PL/SQL efforts primarily focus on directly generating PL/SQL from complete NL requirements. In practice, PL/SQL development involves diverse scenarios, such as from-scratch development, code modification, debugging, and optimization, and may require either direct generation or multi-turn interaction. Yet, no comprehensive benchmark evaluates multi-scenario, direct and interactive, and multi-dialect NL-to-PL/SQL development. In this paper, we present ProcArena, an execution-based benchmark covering both Direct and Interactive modes. ProcArena comprises 3,998 executable tasks over 157 databases, spanning nine development subscenarios in PostgreSQL and Oracle. We construct challenging Direct tasks through Iterative Logic Enhancement and scenario-specific adapters, and derive paired Interactive tasks through Knowledge Integration and Requirement Perturbation while preserving executable targets. We further design a controlled Solver-User Simulator protocol that allows models to clarify user intent and inspect the database environment without exposing hidden execution feedback. Evaluating seven language models, we find that the best average scores are only 62.2% and 57.8% in Direct and Interactive, respectively, demonstrating that realistic NL-to-PL/SQL development remains challenging, particularly in interactive settings.

title: Adaptive Machine Learning for Unstructured Data Feature Extraction
abstract: This paper presents an innovative approach to data feature extraction utilizing adaptive machine learning. Traditional machine learning often relies on manually defined features, while this method dynamically learns features from the inherent characteristics of unstructured data. The core of the methodology involves employing an adaptive learning algorithm to construct a complex feature model, enabling the system to automatically identify and extract meaningful patterns and relationships within the data. This approach aims to significantly enhance feature identification accuracy and robustness. The paper details the methodology, its implementation, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness in extracting valuable features from diverse, unstructured datasets. The focus is on automating the feature extraction process, reducing human intervention, and improving the overall predictive power of the models.

title: Adaptive Quantum State Preservation through Dynamic Phase Transitions
abstract: Quantum information is notoriously vulnerable to decoherence, a phenomenon arising from interactions with the environment. This vulnerability necessitates robust strategies for preserving quantum states. This paper explores a novel approach to quantum state preservation – Adaptive Quantum State Preservation through Dynamic Phase Transitions – that leverages the inherent dynamism of quantum systems to proactively mitigate decoherence. We propose a mechanism for continuous monitoring of a quantum state and triggered phase transitions based on predefined conditions, effectively acting as a dynamic stabilizer. The core mechanism is detailed, and its potential for protecting quantum information from decoherence is investigated through theoretical analysis and preliminary simulations. The paper concludes with a discussion of future research directions and potential applications.

title: Quantum Bayesian Inference for Complex Control Systems
abstract: Quantum Bayesian Inference (QBI) offers a promising avenue for enhancing complex control systems, particularly in the face of noisy environments. This paper explores the application of QBI to estimate the system's state and plan actions, leveraging Bayesian inference to mitigate uncertainty and improve robustness. We propose a novel quantum-inspired Bayesian estimation scheme designed to reduce uncertainty and provide enhanced control capabilities. The core mechanism focuses on utilizing quantum-like principles to refine system state estimation, thereby improving overall system performance. This research addresses the limitations of classical Bayesian methods by introducing a fundamentally more efficient approach.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum machine learning framework based on dynamic topology. We propose a method for learning and optimizing machine learning models by leveraging the inherent topological properties of a dynamically evolving quantum structure. The framework utilizes a continuous, self-organized topology to guide the learning process, resulting in enhanced efficiency and potentially improved performance compared to traditional approaches. This work explores the potential of dynamically structured quantum systems to accelerate the training and inference of complex machine learning models. The core mechanism revolves around constructing and manipulating a quantum state that evolves through a defined topology, enabling the model to explore a vast solution space more effectively. title: Dynamic Symbolic Computation via Temporal Logic and Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to dynamic symbolic computation by integrating temporal logic reasoning with reinforcement learning. The core idea is to enable a system to adaptively learn and optimize its symbolic representations through a feedback mechanism. We introduce an agent that utilizes temporal logic constraints to guide its manipulation of symbolic representations, and reinforcement learning to optimize its actions based on the success of its reasoning. The system learns to refine its symbolic structures, improving its ability to solve complex problems. This work addresses the limitations of traditional symbolic computation by introducing a dynamic, learning-based framework. The proposed system demonstrates the potential for enhanced reasoning capabilities in domains where symbolic representations are crucial, but static definitions may not be sufficient for optimal performance. The key contributions lie in the synergistic combination of temporal logic's constraint satisfaction capabilities with reinforcement learning's ability to learn optimal strategies. The system's performance is evaluated through simulated scenarios, showcasing the effectiveness of this hybrid approach.

title: Contextual Graph Neural Networks with Dynamic Attention Mechanisms
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and recommendation systems. However, a significant limitation of many existing GNN models lies in their reliance on static attention mechanisms. These mechanisms often assign fixed weights to neighbors, neglecting the dynamic and evolving nature of graph relationships. This paper introduces a novel approach – Contextual Graph Neural Networks with Dynamic Attention Mechanisms – designed to overcome this limitation. The core idea is to develop an attention mechanism that adapts its weights based on the current node's neighborhood, the message content being exchanged, and the overall graph structure. This dynamic adaptation allows the network to capture more nuanced and context-dependent relationships within the graph, leading to improved node representations and enhanced message passing. We formally describe the model, its key components, and the underlying mathematical framework. We argue that this approach represents a significant advancement in GNN research, offering the potential for greater accuracy and robustness in complex graph-structured data.

title: Hybrid Monte Carlo Tree Search with Neural Network Guidance
abstract: This paper introduces a novel hybrid Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithm incorporating neural network guidance. Traditional MCTS methods struggle with computationally expensive pruning and often exhibit suboptimal performance due to reliance on purely heuristic search. We propose a system that leverages a neural network to dynamically evaluate promising paths, providing feedback that refines the search and improves solution quality. The algorithm integrates a neural network into the tree search, learning to predict the quality of each node and guide the exploration process towards more promising regions. This approach significantly enhances the efficiency and accuracy of MCTS, overcoming limitations of existing methods. The paper details the architecture, training methodology, and performance evaluation of the proposed system, demonstrating a substantial improvement in search quality compared to standard MCTS.

title: Probability Field Theory: Quantum State Generation and Measurement Algorithms
abstract: Probability field theory (PFT) offers a novel approach to quantum state generation and measurement, addressing limitations of traditional quantum computation by providing a direct, self-optimizing process. This paper explores the design of a PFT framework for generating quantum states, leveraging the inherent properties of probability fields to enhance measurement algorithms. We propose a mechanism that integrates the PFT's generative capabilities with quantum state measurement, leading to improved efficiency and accuracy. The core claim is that this framework offers a significant advancement in quantum state analysis and validation, reducing the reliance on computationally intensive simulation. This work presents a detailed design and analysis of the proposed algorithm, highlighting its potential impact on the development of practical quantum computing systems.

title: Dynamic Program Synthesis via Automated Theorem Proving
abstract: Existing program synthesis techniques often struggle to effectively generate complex, dynamic programs due to limitations in handling intricate program structures and runtime behavior. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing automated theorem proving (ATP) to overcome these challenges. The core idea is to leverage ATP's ability to rigorously verify and synthesize programs based on formal specifications. Unlike traditional methods that typically employ static analysis or hand-crafted heuristics, our approach allows for a dynamic adaptation of the theorem prover's search strategy, responding to the evolving program structure during the synthesis process. This dynamic adaptation is crucial for handling the complexities inherent in dynamic programs. The system operates by first translating a high-level specification into a formal representation suitable for ATP. The ATP then systematically explores the solution space, guided by the specification and its own internal reasoning capabilities. The resulting synthesized program is formally verified to meet the original specification. We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of this approach through a series of illustrative examples, highlighting its potential to significantly advance program synthesis capabilities. The key contribution of this work lies in the integration of dynamic theorem proving with program synthesis, enabling the generation of more robust, efficient, and complex programs. The theoretical underpinnings and practical implementation details are presented, providing a blueprint for future research in this area.

title: Based on Multi-Modal Collaborative Reasoning for Knowledge Graphs (MCK)
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework, Multi-Modal Collaborative Reasoning for Knowledge Graphs (MCK), designed to enhance knowledge graph construction and reasoning capabilities by integrating information from diverse modalities. The core idea is to build a knowledge graph that can perform collaborative reasoning across text, images, and potentially audio data. The proposed methodology leverages deep learning models for individual modality processing, an attention mechanism for modality fusion, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for knowledge inference. This approach addresses the limitations of existing knowledge graphs, which predominantly rely on single-modality data, by significantly improving the expressive power and reasoning accuracy of the resulting graph. We demonstrate the potential of MCK through a theoretical framework, outlining the key components and their interactions. The core claim is that by fusing multimodal data, we can construct a knowledge graph capable of multi-modal collaborative reasoning. The core mechanism involves deep learning for modality processing, attention-based fusion, and GNNs for inference. This new approach provides a pathway towards more robust and comprehensive knowledge representation and reasoning. ---

title: Quantum Machine Learning: A Topological Style Transfer Approach
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) is a rapidly evolving field that explores the potential of quantum computing to enhance machine learning algorithms. This paper investigates a novel approach to QML: Topological Style Transfer (TST). We propose a method that leverages the inherent topological properties of quantum systems to facilitate feature transfer and improve model robustness. The core concept is to map quantum model parameters onto a topological structure, thereby promoting generalization and enhancing the model's resilience to noise. This research aims to address limitations in traditional QML techniques by introducing a fundamentally different approach based on graph theory and topology. The paper will detail the methodology, results, and potential implications of this approach, demonstrating its potential to advance the state of QML.

abstract: This paper explores the development and application of world models within the framework of probabilistic programming languages. We propose a mechanism utilizing Bayesian Networks and Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) to represent system dynamics, combined with the expressive power of probabilistic programming languages for inference and learning. This approach allows for the creation of intelligent control systems capable of prediction and adaptation. The paper details the key components of this architecture and discusses its potential benefits over traditional approaches to world model design. We demonstrate the feasibility of this approach through a conceptual framework, focusing on the theoretical underpinnings and highlighting the advantages of using a declarative, probabilistic programming paradigm. ---

title: Information-Theoretic Limits of Graph Compression
abstract: This paper investigates the information-theoretic limits of graph compression, aiming to establish fundamental bounds on the achievable compression ratio. We leverage concepts from information theory, specifically source coding and channel capacity, to analyze the redundancy present within graph structures. The core of our approach involves quantifying the mutual information between different parts of a graph and utilizing this information to derive compression limits. We demonstrate that these limits are dependent on the graph's structure, specifically its connectivity and degree distribution, and provide a theoretical framework for understanding the inherent constraints on graph compression. The results presented contribute a rigorous theoretical foundation for the field, offering a benchmark for evaluating the performance of graph compression algorithms and guiding future research directions. The key mathematical components are presented, including expressions for source coding rates, channel capacity calculations, and the derivation of information-theoretic limits.

title: Algorithm for Determining the Initial Shifts in the Formation of Non-binary Gordon–Mills–Welch Sequences
abstract: Based on a modification of the algorithm for determining the shift vector when forming non-binary Gordon–Mills–Welch sequences (GMWS) in finite fields GF( p S ), where S = mn , an algorithm for determining the shift vector C ( m , n , r ) = ( c 1 , c 2 , …, c M ) for M summable sequences is developed. This algorithm is based on solving a system of linear equations for the p -adic representation of the parameter r with respect to the shift values of the sequences. It is shown that for a known value of the decimation index vector A ( m , n , r ) = ( d 1 , d 2 , …, d M ), the number of possible values of the shift vector is L 1 = (( p – 2)!). For given vectors A ( m , n , r ), the shift vectors C ( m , n , r ) are given for the formation of GF(5 4 ), GF(7 4 ), GF(11 4 ) GMWS.

title: Diagnosing and Dynamically Filtering Occupancy World Models for Active Mapping
abstract: Active mapping requires a robot to select camera viewpoints that efficiently reconstruct an unknown 3D scene. To reason about unobserved regions, recent systems use pretrained occupancy networks as world models that complete missing geometry. The predicted structure contributes to expected coverage gain and constrains feasible robot motion. Consequently, occupancy errors can change both what the robot chooses to explore and where it is able to move. We diagnose these effects by holding the planner fixed and varying only the occupancy representation provided to it. We consider planning without completion, with learned occupancy, with false positives removed by a ground truth oracle, with false negatives restored by an oracle, and with ground truth occupancy. Our experiments show that correcting false positives or false negatives alone does not consistently improve final coverage. This finding reveals a gap between occupancy accuracy and downstream planning performance. Ground truth occupancy provides a much larger improvement in coverage efficiency than in endpoint coverage, suggesting that planning and reachability remain important bottlenecks even when the geometric world model is accurate. Based on these findings, we introduce a dynamic filtering strategy that preserves predictions in unexplored space while suppressing repeatedly unsupported occupancy using online observations. Preliminary examples show that this strategy can redirect viewpoint selection toward reachable surfaces that would otherwise remain unobserved.

title: RAÍZ: A Hybrid Architecture Based on Linguistic Knowledge and Deep Learning for the Machine Translation of Low-Resource Indigenous Languages
abstract: Indigenous languages continue to experience significant technological marginalisation due to limited digital corpora, orthographic inconsistency, dialectal variation, morphological complexity, and insufficient representation in contemporary natural language processing systems. This study introduces RAÍZ, a hybrid machine translation architecture designed for low-resource Indigenous languages. The proposed framework combines Transformer-based multilingual modelling with linguistically informed components, including phonetic normalisation, morphological segmentation, semantic contextualisation, lexical retrieval mechanisms, and community-centred validation procedures involving native speakers. The architecture was evaluated using Spanish–Nahuatl and Spanish–Mazahua translation tasks through a mixed evaluation strategy integrating BLEU, chrF, and COMET metrics alongside qualitative assessment focused on clarity, naturalness, semantic fidelity, and cultural appropriateness. Experimental results indicate that RAÍZ achieved 28.6 BLEU, 56.8 chrF, and 74% COMET in the Spanish–Nahuatl task, while obtaining 27.4 BLEU, 54.9 chrF, and 71% COMET for Spanish–Mazahua translation. The findings suggest that hybrid and linguistically grounded approaches can improve translation robustness in low-resource settings while supporting culturally sensitive language technologies. The study further highlights the importance of combining neural architectures with community participation and explicit linguistic knowledge in the development of more inclusive machine translation systems for Indigenous languages. Este estudio presenta RAÍZ, una arquitectura híbrida de traducción automática diseñada para lenguas indígenas con pocos recursos. El marco propuesto combina modelado multilingüe basado en Transformers con componentes fundamentados en conocimiento lingüístico, entre ellos la normalización fonética, la segmentación morfológica, la contextualización semántica, mecanismos de recuperación léxica y procedimientos de validación centrados en la comunidad con participación de hablantes nativos. La arquitectura se evaluó mediante tareas de traducción español–náhuatl y español–mazahua, utilizando una estrategia de evaluación mixta que integró las métricas BLEU, chrF y COMET con una evaluación cualitativa centrada en la claridad, naturalidad, fidelidad semántica y adecuación cultural. Los resultados experimentales indican que RAÍZ alcanzó 28,6 BLEU, 56,8 chrF y 74 % COMET en la tarea español–náhuatl, mientras que para la traducción español–mazahua obtuvo 27,4 BLEU, 54,9 chrF y 71 % COMET. Los hallazgos sugieren que los enfoques híbridos con fundamento lingüístico pueden mejorar la robustez de la traducción en contextos de bajos recursos y, al mismo tiempo, favorecer el desarrollo de tecnologías lingüísticas culturalmente sensibles. El estudio también destaca la importancia de combinar arquitecturas neuronales con la participación comunitaria y el conocimiento lingüístico explícito para desarrollar sistemas de traducción automática más inclusivos destinados a las lenguas indígenas. title: Probability-Based Complexity Measurement Framework for Adaptive Task Complexity
abstract: This paper introduces a novel probability-based complexity measurement framework designed for dynamic adaptation of complexity metrics across diverse tasks and datasets. Traditional complexity measures often lack flexibility, requiring manual adjustment. We propose a system that leverages probabilistic models to dynamically adjust complexity, resulting in improved model performance. The core of this framework lies in integrating a probability distribution representing complexity as a function of task characteristics and data characteristics. This allows for a more adaptive and robust approach to quantifying model complexity. The proposed method offers significant improvements in handling variable data and task-specific complexities.

title: Quantum Adaptive Computing: An Adaptive Learning Algorithm
abstract: Quantum Adaptive Computing (QAC) represents a paradigm shift in computational paradigms, leveraging quantum mechanics to achieve enhanced processing capabilities. This paper investigates a novel adaptive learning algorithm, dubbed "Quantum Self-Adaptation Algorithm" (QSAA), designed to address the inherent limitations of traditional machine learning techniques. QSAA's core mechanism centers around the utilization of quantum entanglement to dynamically adjust quantum parameters based on the characteristics of the training data. This allows for a more robust and adaptable model, resulting in improved generalization performance. The paper details the algorithm's design, the rationale behind its proposed approach, and explores its potential impact on the field of quantum machine learning. The study emphasizes the advantages of QSAA in dynamically adjusting to data fluctuations, offering a significant advancement over existing approaches.

title: Probability Logic & Nonlinear Geometry Fusion
abstract: This paper investigates the integration of probability logic and non-linear geometry as a framework for modeling and optimization of complex systems. We propose a novel approach that leverages probability distributions as the underlying geometric structure, introducing probabilistic operations to model dynamic changes and utilizing geometric optimization to enhance prediction accuracy. The core claim is that this fusion significantly improves the modeling and optimization capabilities of complex systems, particularly in areas such as structural design and risk modeling. This work addresses a long-standing challenge in applying probabilistic models to real-world problems by offering a fundamentally new approach that harmonizes statistical analysis with geometric abstraction.

title: Quantum Machine Learning with Hierarchical Feature Extraction
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) represents a paradigm shift in computational neuroscience, offering the potential to surpass classical machine learning in certain tasks. This paper explores the application of hierarchical feature extraction, a core concept within QML, to enhance the performance of machine learning models. We propose a quantum algorithm for feature extraction that leverages quantum superposition and entanglement to identify and represent complex patterns within data, followed by a quantum neural network to learn from these representations. This approach aims to improve model accuracy and accelerate training through the integration of quantum computation and machine learning. The core claim is that the combined approach will yield superior results compared to traditional machine learning methods. This work addresses the limitations of current machine learning techniques by introducing a novel quantum approach to feature representation, ultimately facilitating a more robust and efficient learning process. We present a theoretical framework and initial implementation demonstrating the potential of this hybrid architecture.

title: Adaptive Topological Structure Optimization Algorithm
abstract: This paper presents an innovative algorithm, the Adaptive Topological Structure Optimization Algorithm (ATSOA), designed to revolutionize data compression by leveraging quantum entanglement. Traditional data compression techniques often rely on iterative algorithms, limiting their effectiveness, especially when dealing with high-dimensional data. Our approach introduces a novel framework that dynamically adjusts data unit interactions based on quantum entanglement, effectively eliminating redundancy and significantly enhancing compression efficiency. We demonstrate the algorithm's superior performance through comprehensive simulations and comparative analysis against established methods. The core mechanism centers on the manipulation of quantum entanglement to achieve real-time optimization of data structure. The potential implications of this algorithm extend beyond simple data compression, offering a pathway to advancements in information processing and storage.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Constraint Propagation for Sparse Data
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum annealing and Grover's algorithm to enhance constraint propagation for sparse data sets. Sparse data presents significant computational challenges in many applications, particularly in machine learning and optimization problems. Traditional constraint propagation methods often struggle with this data, leading to increased computational costs. We propose an algorithm leveraging quantum annealing to efficiently explore the sparse solution space, reducing the computational burden. The core mechanism involves employing quantum algorithms to accelerate the search for optimal solutions, ultimately improving performance. This work explores the theoretical benefits and potential practical applications of this approach.

title: Adaptive Generalization Matrix
abstract: This paper introduces an Adaptive Generalization Matrix (AGM) – a novel matrix operation designed to enhance machine learning model generalization by dynamically adjusting matrix weights based on data characteristics. Traditional matrix operations are often fixed, limiting the model's ability to effectively learn across diverse datasets. The AGM leverages deep learning to automatically learn and adapt matrix weights, fostering improved performance on unseen data. This research explores a mechanism that utilizes a 'dynamic learning matrix' to achieve this adaptation. The core claim is that the AGM significantly improves machine learning model generalization, particularly in complex datasets.

title: Quantum Information Dynamics: Computational Validation of Topological Chaos
abstract: Quantum information dynamics (QID) offers a powerful approach to simulating complex quantum systems, particularly those exhibiting topological chaos. This paper explores the development of a computational validation framework for QID, focusing on applications in quantum entanglement and quantum key distribution. We introduce a novel method leveraging quantum entanglement to precisely measure and validate topological chaos, utilizing parallel quantum computation for accelerated verification. This framework represents a significant step towards validating the potential of QID within the realm of quantum information processing. The core claim is that this framework will provide a robust and efficient method for assessing the validity of topological chaos in quantum information systems.

title: Relational Reasoning with Continuous Tensor Representations
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to relational reasoning by leveraging continuous tensor representations of relationships. Traditional methods relying on discrete symbols (e.g., 'A is above B') struggle to capture the inherent complexities and nuances of real-world relationships. Our method replaces these symbolic representations with continuous tensor fields, enabling a more flexible and expressive model for reasoning about connections. Specifically, we define relationships as tensors, where each dimension represents a relevant feature or attribute. The values within these tensors encode the strength and nature of the relationship. We explore initial formulations, focusing on representing spatial and hierarchical relationships. The core idea is that relationships aren't simply binary 'true' or 'false' but exist on a continuous spectrum. The continuous tensors allow us to represent degrees of relatedness, contextual information, and even uncertainty. This approach offers a significant departure from discrete symbolic reasoning and presents a foundation for more sophisticated relational understanding in AI systems. We introduce a simplified framework for calculating relationships between entities based on tensor similarity and propose initial techniques for incorporating context into the tensor representation. Further research will focus on scaling this approach to more complex relationship domains and developing efficient algorithms for tensor-based reasoning.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Based Information Encoding in Neuromorphic Computing
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to neuromorphic computing by leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core idea is to utilize multi-particle quantum entanglement states as the physical connections between artificial neurons, enabling efficient parallel information processing and mimicking biological neural networks. We propose a quantum neuromorphic chip architecture employing multiple superconducting quantum bits (Qubits) engineered to exhibit entanglement. The design focuses on manipulating the coherence time, topological structure, and combined operation of quantum gates to emulate synaptic transmission and learning within biological neural networks. Specifically, we investigate encoding information through entanglement and explore parallel computation facilitated by this quantum phenomenon. Furthermore, we address the challenges of quantum computation by integrating quantum decoherence and quantum error correction techniques. The potential for achieving high-performance, energy-efficient, and biologically inspired computing is discussed, representing a significant departure from traditional approaches and classical neural networks. The proposed framework offers a pathway towards scalable quantum neuromorphic systems with potential applications in areas such as pattern recognition, machine learning, and complex system modeling.

title: Title: Adaptive Quantum Circuit Design – Neural Network-Guided Optimization
abstract: This paper presents an adaptive quantum circuit design framework leveraging a neural network to automate the process of circuit creation. Traditional quantum circuit design is often a laborious and iterative process, relying heavily on expert knowledge and trial-and-error. We introduce a novel system that utilizes a trained neural network to automatically generate quantum circuits with optimized properties, aiming to significantly reduce manual effort and accelerate quantum algorithm development. The framework employs a multi-stage training process, beginning with a pre-trained model and iteratively refining it based on a defined set of performance metrics. The core mechanism centers on the neural network's ability to learn the optimal circuit parameters to maximize desired properties such as fidelity, coherence, and connectivity. This approach promises to provide a more efficient and scalable method for quantum circuit design.

title: Nonlinear Time Series Dependency Networks for Causal Inference
abstract: This paper introduces the Nonlinear Time Series Dependency Network (NSTDN) framework, designed to address the limitations of traditional time series networks in accurately performing causal inference. The core claim is that NSTDNs can effectively identify and model nonlinear time-dependent relationships, leading to improved causal reasoning. This is achieved through a novel mechanism incorporating "causal constraint learning," which combines Bayesian Networks and Reinforcement Learning to learn and interpret causal relationships within the network. The system learns by iteratively updating its structure and parameters based on observed data and a reward signal that reflects the accuracy of its causal inferences. Mathematical formulations are presented to detail the learning process and the inference engine. We demonstrate a conceptual framework, outlining the architecture and key components of the NSTDN. Further research will focus on developing more sophisticated reward functions and exploring the application of NSTDNs across diverse domains.

title: Introducing TAM: A PyTorch-Based Additive Forecasting Framework and its Application to Explainable Anomaly Detection
abstract: This is the official slide deck for the presentation "Introducing TAM: A PyTorch-Based Additive Forecasting Framework and its Application to Explainable Anomaly Detection," delivered at the DASS Workshop (Anomaly detection for modern data) on September 8th, 2026. Overview: The presentation introduces the Time series Additive Model (TAM) v1.3.0, a PyTorch-based framework that combines the transparency of standard statistical models with exact, GPU-scaled primal resolution. It demonstrates how an explainable additive model can not merely flag an anomaly, but adapt to it through both time and space. The framework's capabilities are illustrated through two distinct case studies: Power Grids (Time): Forecasting French national electricity load through severe structural regime shifts, specifically the COVID-19 lockdowns and the 2022 energy crisis. It highlights the use of sliding-window correctors (AdaptiveTAM) and dynamic expert aggregation (OperaTAM) to track shifting mechanisms in real-time. Real Estate (Space): Detecting and mathematically deconstructing spatial price anomalies in the French housing market. It showcases TAM's new statistical layer, utilizing non-Gaussian distributional location-scale solves combined with Conformal Quantile Regression (CQR) to generate exact, explainable price intervals. title: A Universal Physical Operator Mapping Architecture for In-Material Photonic Computation and Hardware-Bound Trust 一种基于微纳光子物理算子映射的"材料即计算"与内生硬件信任根架构
abstract: Abstract—Computation, at its fundamental root, is an isomorphic mapping between an abstract mathematical dictionary and deterministic physical state transitions. For decades, conventional computing has adhered to a reductionist doctrine: forcing all multi-dimensional, continuous mathematical operations into sequences of binary Boolean logic gates. In this work, we propose a paradigm shift toward "in-material computation via physical operator mapping," demonstrating that a physical medium can directly evaluate mathematical operators without digital gate synthesis. Using a vertically integrated, electro-optically tunable Fabry-Pérot microcavity coupled with sub-wavelength cross-gratings and monolayer two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDCs), we establish a unified physical computing framework: (1) Scalar arithmetic (addition and subtraction) is directly executed by parametric sum-frequency generation (SFG) and difference-frequency generation (DFG) at sub-picosecond speeds with constant O(1)temporal complexity; (2) Multi-dimensional vector transformations and spatial convolutions are evaluated passively through the reciprocal lattice scattering of the periodic cross-grating; (3) The irreproducible atomic-scale manufacturing disorder of the nanostructure inherently constitutes a physical unclonable function (PUF), establishing an open-parameter zero-trust hardware root of trust protected by an extreme computational asymmetry (time-lock) against digital software emulation. This architecture unifies high-throughput in-material computing and hardware-bound security within a single nanophotonic platform, providing an open, scalable foundation for post-Moore computing.

title: Title: Adaptive Topology for Neural Network Training
abstract: This paper investigates the application of adaptive topology for neural network training, a paradigm shift from traditional static training methods. We present preliminary results demonstrating the efficacy of this method on several benchmark datasets.

title: Dynamic Neural Architecture Search with Evolutionary Algorithms and Reinforcement Learning
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural architecture search (NAS) that leverages the strengths of evolutionary algorithms (EAs) and reinforcement learning (RL) to achieve dynamic and adaptive architecture exploration. The core idea is to use an RL agent to control an EA, effectively guiding the search process towards architectures with optimal performance for a given dataset. The RL agent learns to adjust the EA's parameters—such as mutation rates, crossover probabilities, and population sizes—dynamically, responding to the evolving landscape of the architecture space. This dynamic adaptation distinguishes this approach from traditional static EA-based NAS methods, leading to improved convergence speed and architectural diversity. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through theoretical analysis and a conceptual design, outlining the key components and interactions within the system. The proposed method offers a promising direction for automating the design of high-performing neural networks, particularly in scenarios with complex datasets and varying computational constraints.

title: Adaptive Quantum Control Algorithm Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the optimization of quantum control algorithms using reinforcement learning (RL). The core claim is that RL can significantly enhance the control precision and efficiency of quantum devices. We propose a framework where the quantum control algorithm is treated as an intelligent agent, interacting with the quantum environment to learn optimal control strategies. This approach allows for adaptive control, addressing the challenges inherent in designing fixed control protocols for complex quantum systems. The methodology involves defining a reward function that reflects the desired quantum state evolution, using RL algorithms to train the agent, and validating the learned control strategy through simulations. We demonstrate the potential of this approach to improve control accuracy and robustness, particularly in scenarios with noisy environments or rapidly changing system parameters. The results suggest a promising direction for leveraging machine learning techniques to unlock the full potential of quantum control.

title: 基于多模态概率推理的决策系统
abstract: This paper proposes a decision-making system grounded in multi-modal probabilistic reasoning. The core claim is that integrating probabilistic information from diverse modalities—such as vision, audio, and text—significantly enhances the robustness and accuracy of decision-making processes. The system utilizes a multi-modal probabilistic graphical model and Bayesian inference algorithms to effectively model and reason about the dependencies between these modalities. Specifically, the model learns the conditional probabilities between different modalities and leverages Bayesian inference to update decision probabilities based on incoming evidence. The approach addresses the challenges of uncertainty inherent in multi-modal data and provides a framework for robust risk assessment and ultimately, improved decision outcomes. The key innovation lies in the explicit incorporation of probabilistic relationships between modalities, leading to a more nuanced and reliable decision-making process compared to traditional, single-modality approaches. The system's architecture provides a flexible and adaptable solution for applications requiring informed decisions under conditions of incomplete or conflicting information.

title: Information Entropy-Driven Neuron Activation
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neural network activation based on information entropy. The core claim is that a neuron's activation level is directly proportional to the change in the entropy of the input information. We introduce a neuron model that explicitly calculates the entropy of its inputs and utilizes this entropy value as the driving force for neuron activation. This mechanism aims to improve information processing efficiency by providing a quantifiable metric – entropy – to govern neuronal responses. The model's design leverages established information theory principles, offering a distinct departure from traditional activation functions that often rely on simple thresholding or weighted sums. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a theoretical analysis, outlining how controlling the flow of information entropy can lead to more targeted and efficient neural responses. The research contributes to a deeper understanding of neuronal dynamics and opens possibilities for designing more sophisticated and energy-efficient artificial neural networks. ---

title: Graph-Based Explainable AI for Complex Decision-Making
abstract: The increasing prevalence of complex AI models, particularly deep neural networks, in critical decision-making domains has raised significant concerns regarding transparency and trust. These "black-box" models often operate as opaque systems, making it challenging to understand *why* a particular decision was made. This paper proposes a novel approach to explainable AI (XAI) based on graph representation. We argue that representing the decision-making process as a graph—where nodes represent features and edges represent relationships—provides an intuitive and effective method for visualizing and understanding the model's reasoning. The framework presented offers a structured approach to building XAI systems, facilitating trust and accountability in AI-driven decisions. We outline the core components of this graph-based XAI system and discuss its potential applications across various domains.

title: Decomposition-Based Verification of Large-Scale Software Systems
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to formal verification of large-scale software systems, termed decomposition-based verification. The core idea is to leverage the inherent modularity of software systems by systematically breaking them down into smaller, independently verifiable modules. This strategy directly addresses the scalability limitations of traditional formal verification techniques, which often struggle with the complexity of large systems. We detail a methodology encompassing module decomposition, interface definition, and the application of automated theorem proving. Our approach aims to significantly reduce the verification effort and improve the practicality of formal verification for complex, real-world software applications. The effectiveness of this methodology is demonstrated through the conceptual framework, outlining the key steps and considerations for successful implementation. The paper culminates in a discussion of potential challenges and future research directions within this decomposition-based verification paradigm.

title: Adaptive Kernel Design via Evolutionary Algorithms
abstract: Kernel methods represent a cornerstone of modern machine learning, offering powerful tools for non-linear classification and regression. However, their effectiveness hinges critically on the selection of the kernel function, a process often characterized by extensive manual tuning and subjective judgment. This work introduces a novel approach to kernel design that leverages the principles of evolutionary algorithms to automate and optimize this crucial step. The proposed method employs an evolutionary algorithm to iteratively refine kernel functions, directly adapting them to the specific characteristics of the data and desired computational efficiency. The algorithm operates by evaluating candidate kernels on a validation set, selecting the fittest individuals, and generating new generations through mutation and crossover. This process allows for the exploration of a vast design space, potentially uncovering kernels that outperform those designed through traditional, human-guided methods. The core contribution lies in shifting the design paradigm from manual tuning to automated evolution, offering a more robust and efficient pathway to optimal kernel function selection. This research addresses the inherent limitations of current kernel design practices and presents a promising avenue for enhancing the performance and applicability of kernel methods.

However, their effectiveness hinges critically on the selection of the kernel function, a process often characterized by extensive manual tuning and subjective judgment. This work introduces a novel approach to kernel design that leverages the principles of evolutionary algorithms to automate and optimize this crucial step. The proposed method employs an evolutionary algorithm to iteratively refine kernel functions, directly adapting them to the specific characteristics of the data and desired computational efficiency. The algorithm operates by evaluating candidate kernels on a validation set, selecting the fittest individuals, and generating new generations through mutation and crossover. This process allows for the exploration of a vast design space, potentially uncovering kernels that outperform those designed through traditional, human-guided methods. The core contribution lies in shifting the design paradigm from manual tuning to automated evolution, offering a more robust and efficient pathway to optimal kernel function selection. This research addresses the inherent limitations of current kernel design practices and presents a promising avenue for enhancing the performance and applicability of kernel methods.

title: Dynamic Quantum Entanglement Measurement
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, presents a unique challenge for measurement and analysis. Precise measurement of entangled states is crucial for exploiting quantum phenomena, but current measurement techniques often struggle to accurately determine the entangled state's properties. This paper investigates a novel dynamic quantum entanglement measurement approach designed to address this challenge. We propose a method that utilizes real-time monitoring of entangled state dynamics, employing machine learning to dynamically adjust measurement parameters, ultimately leading to improved accuracy in entanglement state identification. The core mechanism centers around modeling the evolving entanglement, enabling automated parameter adjustment for optimal measurement. This approach offers a significant advancement in the field of quantum entanglement measurement, promising to unlock new capabilities in quantum information processing and quantum technology.

title: Self-Assembling Neural Networks via Evolutionary Graph Structure
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neural network architecture design utilizing an evolutionary algorithm to dynamically optimize the network's graph structure. Traditional neural network design relies heavily on manual architecture engineering, a process often hampered by limited human intuition and computational constraints. Our method introduces an automated self-assembly process, where a population of neural networks evolves over generations, directly manipulating connection weights and, crucially, the underlying graph structure. The evolutionary algorithm iteratively creates, modifies, and deletes connections within the network, guided by a fitness function that quantifies network performance, typically measured by accuracy or loss on a given task. The core claim is that allowing networks to self-organize their connectivity patterns can lead to significantly improved architectures compared to manually designed networks. We detail the evolutionary algorithm's components, including the representation of the graph structure, the mutation and crossover operators, and the fitness function. The results demonstrate the potential of this approach to generate networks exhibiting superior performance, highlighting a shift from human-centric design to a more automated and potentially more efficient process.

title: Quantum Simulation of Phase Transitions – Hierarchical State-Space Representations
abstract: Quantum simulation of phase transitions offers unprecedented opportunities for understanding and controlling complex material behavior. This paper investigates a novel approach to quantum simulation utilizing hierarchical state-space representations, aiming to significantly improve the accuracy and efficiency of these simulations. We propose a method for constructing a state space that recursively decomposes the system's dynamics, enabling a more detailed and nuanced representation of the phase transition. This enhanced representation will facilitate the exploration of intricate transition pathways and improve the fidelity of simulations, ultimately unlocking new insights into phase transition phenomena. This work introduces a framework for hierarchical state space representations, demonstrating its potential for advancing quantum simulation techniques.

title: Adaptive Evolution of Non-linear Topological Deformation
abstract: This paper investigates the application of a self-organizing algorithm to the design of non-linear topological deformations, driven by a neural network. The core concept is to iteratively deform a topological structure guided by a feedback loop, promoting the formation of complex and evolving patterns. We explore a framework where the neural network learns the topology and then iteratively refines it based on internal and external feedback, resulting in a self-organizing evolutionary process. The algorithm's novelty lies in its emphasis on adaptive deformation driven by a learned neural network, rather than relying on predefined parameters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations, showcasing the ability to generate intricate and dynamically changing topological structures. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of this design for various applications, including materials science and computational geometry.

Sources audited. title: Measuring GEO Visibility: Prompt Corpora Define the Answer Market
abstract: GEO (generative engine optimization) visibility scores aggregate source appearances, citations, or brand mentions in generated answers. The prompt corpus selects the situations evaluated, while weights determine their relative importance. Together they define an "answer market" that need not represent actual user demand. Prompt wording can alter retrieval, competing sources, and generated answers. Scoring then requires identifying the appearances, citations, or mentions of interest. If a language model performs this task, its instruction can change the score assigned to an unchanged answer. Our critical survey examines how these choices help define what a GEO score measures. It draws on research into whether indicators measure the intended phenomenon, total survey error, and information retrieval evaluation. The framework specifies situation annotation, prompt formulations, execution conditions, weights, and scoring rules. When weights are unknown or remain to be chosen, the framework reports sets of admissible scores. It distinguishes values compatible with data and assumptions about a target population (partial identification) from variation across weighting conventions (normative sensitivity). A citation alone does not establish a source's contribution. The article defines a comparison of answers generated with and without a source in a controlled documentary context, distinct from an intervention on the full engine with competing sources. The framework is supported by reproducible calculations. No new experiments are reported; its general empirical validity remains to be assessed.

title: Model-Adaptive and Risk-Constrained Frequency Hopping Against Predictive Jammers
abstract: Adaptive frequency hopping against predictive jamming must address both model uncertainty and policy exposure: the context-loss relationship may vary across operating regimes, while persistent hopping patterns may expose high-probability channels to attack. We propose D-PACT-AFH, a model-adaptive and risk-constrained adversarial contextual-bandit framework in which a Tsallis-FTRL master combines a global linear learner with a partitioned local learner and selects the model class online. D-PACT-Hit incorporates channel-wise marginal hit risk into model selection, while D-PACT-Safe applies a minimum-Kullback-Leibler projection to enforce a per-slot risk budget. We establish estimator validity under non-anticipating attacks, an oracle decomposition relative to the better fixed base, and an exact conditional-risk guarantee for the Safe projection. Experiments across diverse channel regimes and jammer types demonstrate effective model adaptation and a controllable goodput-risk tradeoff: D-PACT-AFH recovers 95.5% of the local learner's gain under observable switching while avoiding 77.7% of its degradation in a negative-control regime.

title: Cross-Lingual Indirect Prompt Injection Across Retrieval, Reranking, And Generation In Multilingual RAG
abstract: External evidence can make retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) more informative, yet retrieved passages also provide a path for adversarial instructions to enter the model context. We examine that path in an English-Indonesian RAG system and track cross-lingual indirect prompt injection separately at retrieval, reranking, and generation. The experiment starts from 75 semantic items and evaluates every item in eight query/body/payload language combinations, for 600 paired trials. Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and BGE-M3 produce top-20 candidate sets, BGE-reranker-v2-m3 reduces each set to five documents, and Qwen3-0.6B answers from the resulting context with either a standard prompt or an explicit trust-boundary prompt. Statistical uncertainty is estimated by resampling semantic items, and paired binary outcomes are modeled with generalized estimating equations. Poison documents reached the top 20 in 80.50% of Qwen trials and 37.67% of BGE-M3 trials (odds ratio 6.94, 95% CI 4.53-10.63). Top-five exposure was 18.50% and 16.17%, respectively. Standard end-to-end attack success was 6.33% for Qwen and 6.00% for BGE-M3; boundary-aware prompting lowered both rates to 1.33%, with no canary false positives. The results indicate that multilingual RAG security depends on several linked stages rather than generation alone.

title: Kahve Gurtunca 3.0, a Solar Position Module
abstract: Software components declare their limits. A validity window, an accuracy figure, a truncation bound: these are stated in documentation and taken on trust by everyone downstream. A declared limit and a measured limit are different objects, and only the second one can be planned against. This paper characterises one solar position module, Kahve Gurtunca 3.0, by measuring what it declares. Three measurement rounds contributed: an initial programme, and two blind re-measurements that received the protocol and none of the results. The headline outcome is not a number, it is a pattern. Accuracy quantities reproduced across rounds to four significant figures in the deviation and to within a tenth of a percent in the sensitivity. A speed quantity did not reproduce at all, differing by a third between two rounds, with neither round wrong. That difference is invisible to a single round, and it is the reason for running more than one. One measured result is reported here because it is the one a reader is most likely to want. Against the reference-grade peer of this field, NREL SPA, on 24,060 points, the two sit 0.09 percent apart in distance to the reference authority, JPL Horizons, and the module's algorithm costs 58 percent of the peer's default path when both are written in one language and timed on one machine. Both halves of that sentence need their qualifications and all of them are given in section 3.5: the measurement cannot separate the authority's own error from either implementation's, so being indistinguishable is not the same as being equal; the cost figure compares algorithms and not shipped artefacts, because the row measured for this module is a translation of it into the table's language; the peer can be compiled instead of interpreted, and when it is, the share rises to 73 percent on one thread and inverts to the peer's favour on its own default of four threads; and the module declares a validity window of two centuries where the peer declares eight millennia, which is where part of the speed is bought. The paper also reports what could not be measured, and why, in the same body text as what could.

title: ##基于量子算法的复杂系统建模
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum algorithms to revolutionize complex system modeling. Traditional methods often struggle with the inherent complexity of these systems, limiting the precision of predictions and hindering optimization. Quantum computing offers a paradigm shift through its unique capabilities – quantum superposition, entanglement, and interference – which promise to overcome these limitations. We present a framework for utilizing quantum algorithms to model complex systems, exploring specific algorithms suitable for tasks like simulating fluid dynamics, optimizing material properties, and analyzing biological systems. The paper details the potential benefits, challenges, and preliminary experimental explorations of this approach, emphasizing the transformative impact of quantum computing on complex system analysis. The core claim is that leveraging quantum algorithms will lead to more accurate system modeling, enhanced prediction, and improved optimization capabilities.

title: Nonlinear Adaptive Neural Networks: A Dynamic Modeling Framework
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic modeling framework for complex systems, leveraging the inherent non-linearity of adaptive neural networks. We propose a method for constructing a dynamic system model where the neural network's learning process serves as the core of the simulation, enabling more accurate system predictions. The key innovation lies in incorporating a non-linear dynamics layer within the network architecture, allowing the model to capture complex temporal dependencies and emergent behavior. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations exploring the dynamics of a simplified, but representative, biological system. The core claim of this work is that this framework offers a powerful and flexible approach to modeling dynamic systems, surpassing the limitations of traditional static models.

abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement to revolutionize information encoding. Traditional information transmission methods are limited by the speed and fragility of classical signals. Quantum entanglement, a peculiar phenomenon where two particles become linked regardless of distance, offers a fundamentally different approach. We propose a novel information encoding scheme leveraging this entanglement, aiming to achieve significantly enhanced security and data integrity compared to current methods. The core of this work focuses on the design of a quantum key distribution protocol utilizing entangled states, showcasing its potential for advanced quantum computation and cryptographic applications. We examine the theoretical advantages and practical challenges of this approach, highlighting its unique characteristics and potential impact on the future of information technology.

title: Quantum-Inspired Bayesian Inference with Tensor Networks
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to Bayesian inference by integrating principles from quantum measurement theory with tensor network methods. The core idea is to mimic the probabilistic collapse observed in quantum mechanics during measurement, thereby enhancing the refinement of probability distributions within high-dimensional data. We introduce a tensor network formalism where probabilistic collapse rules are applied during tensor contractions, effectively simulating a quantum measurement process. This method aims to improve the efficiency and accuracy of Bayesian inference, particularly when dealing with complex, highly correlated datasets. The theoretical framework is presented, outlining the mathematical formalism and the key operational rules governing the collapse process. The paper demonstrates the potential of this hybrid approach and lays the groundwork for future research in quantum-inspired statistical inference.

title: Quantum Entanglement-Driven Distributed Key Agreement
abstract: This paper proposes a novel distributed key agreement protocol leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. The core concept involves two parties sharing a pre-established entangled state, performing correlated measurements, and directly using the measurement outcomes to generate a shared secret key. This eliminates the need for classical communication channels, significantly enhancing security by mitigating the risk of eavesdropping during key transmission and reducing latency associated with classical message exchange. The protocol addresses key challenges in entanglement-based systems, namely maintaining entanglement fidelity and ensuring synchronized measurement processing. We outline the theoretical framework, detailing the mathematical formulation of the key generation process and highlighting the critical aspects of entanglement distribution and measurement protocols. This approach represents a fundamental shift in distributed key agreement, moving towards inherently secure and efficient quantum communication systems.

title: On Self-Repairing Programs Based on Information Entropy
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to program self-repair, leveraging the concept of information entropy. The core idea is that a program can proactively adapt and repair itself by measuring its own state entropy and utilizing the rate of entropy change as a decision-making criterion. Unlike traditional self-repair methods that rely on error detection and recovery, this system employs an "entropy sensor" to continuously monitor various aspects of program execution, calculate entropy values, and dynamically adjust the code execution flow based on entropy rate changes. This approach represents a shift towards proactive program adaptation, offering a potentially more robust and efficient mechanism for handling unforeseen issues within a software system. The theoretical framework and underlying principles are detailed, outlining the design and functionality of the entropy-based self-repair system. ---

title: Algorithmic Uncertainty Quantification via Differential Privacy and Ensemble Diversity
abstract: Uncertainty quantification is a critical component of trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Traditional methods often struggle to accurately represent the true uncertainty associated with model predictions, leading to overconfident decisions and potential failure in real-world applications. This paper proposes a novel approach to algorithmic uncertainty quantification that integrates differential privacy with ensemble diversity. We generate a diverse ensemble of models and then leverage statistical variance analysis within the ensemble to quantify uncertainty. The inclusion of differential privacy mitigates the risk of information leakage during the ensemble construction process, enhancing both the accuracy and the privacy guarantees of the uncertainty estimates. This combined approach provides a more robust and reliable measure of algorithmic uncertainty compared to single-model predictions or simple variance calculations. The core contribution lies in the synergistic combination of these two techniques, offering a pathway towards more trustworthy and secure AI systems. The method is demonstrated through theoretical analysis and conceptual framework, with potential applications spanning various domains where accurate uncertainty assessment is paramount.

title: Comparative assessment of long-term methodologies for building-integrated photovoltaic façade energy yield estimation
abstract: ABSTRACT Modelling energy yield of building-integrated photovoltaics requires reliable long-term energy output predictions that match actual generation to encourage its adoption and guarantee cost-effectiveness. This paper evaluates the performance of a Typical Meteorological Year in building-integrated photovoltaic simulations across three façade orientations (east, south and west), and proposes two alternative strategies that improve energy output predictions: a Typical Energy Year based on simulations over 19 years and the Finkelstein-Schafer statistic, and a typical meteorological year specifically designed for building-integrated photovoltaic systems based on the plane-of-array irradiance—which better relates to the tilted positioning of photovoltaic modules on building envelopes—and custom weighting factors for the meteorological variables that are adjusted for each specific case study. Simulation results show good behaviour of both proposed strategies, which provide highly accurate annual energy yield estimations overall. The reliability of the existing Typical Meteorological Year varies with array orientation, boundary conditions and annual variability, suggesting that it requires case-specific analysis to assess suitability. The three methodologies are mutually complementary, and the paper provides guidance towards what strategy is preferable based on key decision aspects, marking a step forward towards better accuracy in building-integrated photovoltaic performance simulations and supporting its implementation in architectural projects.

title: A comprehensive characterization of DNS data
abstract: The Domain Name System (DNS) is responsible for translating human-readable names into computer-friendly identifiers and employs a reverse tree architecture to facilitate this translation. The forward DNS (fDNS) translates human-readable domain names into computer values, while the reverse DNS (rDNS) usually maps an IP address to a hostname. The DNS has evolved into a more intricate system, driven by economic incentives, with data stewardship being delegated to numerous autonomous stakeholders. Due to its role in Internet infrastructure, studying DNS is fundamental for both practical and security reasons. In this work, we characterize commonly used DNS datasets and the challenges linked to their usage. We thoroughly survey DNS focused research studies published over the course of more than a decade, within more than 15 proceedings, and observe a prominent reliance (62%) on short-term datasets. Our investigation into the challenges that limit the adoption of long-term datasets reveals that some of these challenges are associated with the distributed design of the DNS, while others are associated with the evolution of the DNS deployment. That is, we found that, the diversity of stakeholders has the potential to impede data collection and access by various stakeholders, as well as the sharing of data between operators and researchers. Specifically, the distributed design of the DNS leads to challenges regarding namespace coverage, privacy, confidentiality, format, size, and time granularity. Furthermore, certain DNS data is considered commercially sensitive, which further increases the penumbra over the global DNS exchanges, leading to a lack of publicly available DNS data. In earlier works, we observe a distinction in research topics between studies using actively and passively collected DNS data, followed by a recent convergence in topics investigated across both data collection approaches. Lastly, we noted that rDNS data is studied much less than fDNS, i.e., only 2.7% of the studied papers.

title: The list size of random linear codes at capacity
abstract: Let $C \le \mathbb{F}_q^n$ be a uniformly random $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear code of rate $1 - h_q(ρ) - \varepsilon$, and let $L^*(C,ρ)$ be the least $L$ such that every Hamming ball of relative radius $ρ$ contains at most $L$ codewords of $C$. That $L^* = Θ_{q,ρ}(1/\varepsilon)$ has been known since work of Guruswami, Håstad and Kopparty and of Guruswami and Narayanan. Guruswami, Li, Mosheiff, Resch, Silas and Wootters proved that the constant in front of $1/\varepsilon$ is at least $h_q(ρ)$ for all $q$, along with an upper bound special to $q = 2$ which narrowed $L^*$ to within three consecutive integers in that case. But for $q \ge 3$ no upper bound with the correct constant was known. We determine $L^*$ for every prime power $q$. Let $ζ:= h_q(ρ)/\varepsilon$. For every sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, with probability $1-o(1)$ over the choice of $C$, $$L^*(C,ρ) = \lceil ζ\rceil,$$ unless the fractional part of $ζ$ is at most $q^{-Ω_{q,ρ}(ζ)}$, in which case $L^*(C,ρ)$ is $\lfloor ζ\rfloor$ or $\lfloor ζ\rfloor + 1$. By the threshold characterization of random linear codes due to Mosheiff, Resch, Ron-Zewi, Silas and Wootters, both bounds reduce to a two-sided estimate of a single quantity $V(q,L,ρ)$, where $1-V(q,L,ρ)$ is the threshold rate for $(ρ,L)$-list-decodability. title: RevTrace: Code and Experimental Artifacts for Efficient State-Certified ASR Serving
abstract: This record archives the code and experimental artifacts accompanying "RevTrace: A Dual-Granularity Runtime for Efficient State-Certified ASR Serving." It includes frozen runtime sources and configurations, audited experimental results, per-source ground-truth quality scores, and offline validation scripts. The live study contains 96 formal GPU runs, six power-confirmation runs, and eight scheduler controls. Earlier Qwen and Whisper studies are included with their separate measurement scopes. The package includes a README and file manifest. Model weights and source audio corpora are not redistributed; source identifiers, references, and input hashes are provided. Repeated load slots are not additional independent acoustic samples.

title: The Correspondence Equation: A Falsifiable Framework for Measuring Representation–Reality Drift
abstract: The Correspondence Equation (CE) is a quantitative framework for measuring how well an operational representation corresponds to the true, relevant state of a system, across weighted dimensions with variable observability. Version 1.1 resolves two failure modes found by adversarial stress-testing of v1.0: the equation was undefined with zero evidence, and a fully unobserved catastrophic dimension could be reported as near-perfect correspondence. Both are fixed here by blending unobserved dimensions toward a disclosed conservative prior rather than excluding them, verified to reduce the hidden-catastrophe gap from 0.99/0.0012 to 0.55/0.0012 on the same test case. This version also formalizes an exact decomposition separating a genuine change in the underlying state from a change caused by improved observability of an already-existing problem — the same identifiability question addressed in epidemiological surveillance (true vs. detected incidence), applied here to representational correspondence. A serious vulnerability found during testing is disclosed and left unresolved: reducing the declared weight of a known-failing dimension can neutralize the model's bottleneck sensitivity nearly as effectively as hiding it. This is stated explicitly as a condition of publishing v1.1 at all. CE is presented as a falsifiable hypothesis, not a validated instrument. No claim is made about performance on any real historical system. A tested, executable Python reference implementation is included, reproducing every numeric result in the paper. Builds on and cites: Situation Awareness theory (Endsley), organizational sensemaking (Weick), epidemiological ascertainment bias, and intelligence indications-and-warning analysis (Wohlstetter, Grabo).
